REASONS FOR
DECISION

Background

[
1
]

The parties were married on August 15, 1992 and separated on June 20,
2003. Their relationship has been nothing but acrimonious since that time.  The
police have been called on numerous occasions and both parties have been
arrested.  The Halton Children’s Aid Society has been involved with this family
on four separate occasions in addition to Jewish Family and Child Services.

[
2
]

What makes this case more unfortunate is that there are three children
involved, two of whom are dependents.  It is obvious that the children have
been and are being affected by their parent’s behaviour.  Hopefully the
acrimony between the parties will soon dissipate as it is in the children’s
best interest that it does.

[
3
]

Because there were certain issues that required resolution before
Christmas, I gave reasons and certain orders regarding access, the wife’s
proposed change of residence and therapeutic access.  The reasons for my orders
are incorporated into this judgment and the actual orders, previously given in December
2009, are attached as Appendices “A” and “B” for clarity.

[
4
]

In an effort to assist the parties in the future, the issues that I must
decide are as follows:

1.         Although the
wife will be granted sole custody of the children, should she be required to
consult with the husband on issues regarding the children?

2.         Should there
be an order requiring that the children attend for therapeutic access with the
husband at the office of Ms. Michelle Hayes?

3.         Should there
be an order prohibiting the wife from using the children as “go-betweens”?

4.         Should the wife
be ordered to communicate any telephone messages left by the husband to the
children and encourage them to return the phone calls?

5.         Should the
parties be required to communicate via e-mail rather than fax?

6.         Should there
be an equal division of holiday access between the parties (save and except the
summer holidays)?

7.         Should the
wife be entitled to move her residence and if so, should there be a
geographical limitation on such a move?  What should the driving arrangements
be for access visits should the wife move homes?

8.         Should
certain personal property be returned to the husband?

9.         What, if
anything, should happen with the land at T[…] which is jointly owned by the
parties?

10.       Should there
be a refund of child support payments from the wife to the husband for the
period of September, 2003 to early 2004?

11.       Should there
be a refund of child support payments from the wife to the husband for the
period of May, 2007 to September, 2008 when A. was not a dependent?

12.       What income,
if any, should be imputed to the husband for child support purposes?

13.       What amount of
child support should be paid by the husband in the future?

14.       Should the
husband be required to contribute to the children’s private school tuition and
university tuition as an expense pursuant to Section 7 of the
Family Law Act
?

1.

Although the wife will be granted sole custody of the children,
should she be required to consult with the husband on issues regarding the
children?

[
5
]

The parties have agreed that the wife should be granted sole custody of
the children.  However, the dispute arises about whether the parties should
consult each other on certain issues regarding the children.

[
6
]

It is my view that despite the acrimony, the parties should consult with
each other on material items regarding the children such as education and
medical care.  However, the wife shall be responsible for the final decisions
regarding the children and these issues.

[
7
]

I come to the conclusion that the father should be consulted on issues
based on the history of the health of J..  It is clear that in January 2006 J.
disclosed thoughts of injuring himself with a knife.  The wife did not advise
the husband of J.’s thoughts at the time.  The husband learned of the problem
for the first time when he received a Children’s Aid Society (“CAS”) report
regarding other allegations.  This is not appropriate.  A father has a right to
know if one of his children is threatening to hurt himself or herself.  He must
be in a position to assess the situation so that he can provide the support
necessary for his child.

[
8
]

I am further of the view that the husband should be consulted about
major medical decisions because despite J.’s threat to injure himself in
January 2006, as of April 2007 the wife had not accessed the support of a physician
or psychologist to assist J. with his feelings.  As a result, the CAS attended
at the home of the wife and the wife contacted J.’s family doctor when the CAS
advised her to do so and stayed in her home to ensure that it was done.  Had
the husband been aware that J. had not obtained the necessary medical care, he
could either have done so himself or he could have pursued communication with
the wife to ensure that she did so.

[
9
]

Further, there has been much confusion during the last six years
regarding counselling.  I attribute such confusion to the fact that the parties
were not communicating with each other as to what efforts were being made by
them at various times.

[
10
]

For instance, in the fall of 2005, the wife and the children were
involved in a counselling program called “Safety Zone” which is free.  The
husband was not advised that his children were involved in such a program until
after it had begun (and ended).

[
11
]

The husband brought a motion before Horkins J. on March 22, 2006.  He
sought an order that the children attend for counselling with him in Toronto with Dr. Fiati.  It was at the hearing of this motion that the husband learned,
for the first time, that the children had attended Safety Zone.

[
12
]

If the parties were able to consult with each other before counselling
for the children was set up, both parties could participate and there would be
no misconception as to what type of counselling was being sought.  It is in the
best interests of these two children that the parties be able to consult with
each other on issues such as counselling so that their needs are being met and
the parties are able to support them in a most positive way.

[
13
]

I am further of the belief that the father should be consulted with
respect to education.  It appears that J. suffers from learning disabilities.
He is currently in Grade 7 and in a school that is able to accommodate those
needs.  It is hoped that J. will continue to attend his current school until he
graduates from Grade 8.

[
14
]

The decision making that will be critical for any lifetime choices will
occur when the parties are required to decide where to send J. to high school.
The wife testified that she is canvassing technical schools in the area because
she is of the view that J. cannot handle a regular academic high school
curriculum.  Surely this is a decision in which both parents should participate
as it could be life changing for J..  The husband should be consulted on such a
decision.

[
15
]

R. is in Grade 11.  She will be graduating from Grade 12 in 2011.  The
wife testified that R. is very bright and she feels that R. will be able to
accomplish many great things in her life from employment in interior design to
becoming a medical doctor.  Accordingly, the issue of college or university is
one that will have to be confronted shortly.  Again, shouldn’t the husband be
able to participate in such a discussion regarding R.’s post secondary
education?  In my view, the answer is “yes”.

[
16
]

If the parties really do have the best interests of their children in
mind, and I believe that they do, they must put their children first and leave
the acrimony between themselves behind.  To benefit the children, I am ordering
that the wife have sole custody of the children but that the father be
consulted on education and medical issues (including counselling).  The wife
will be the final decision maker regarding these issues.

2.

Should there be an order requiring that the children attend for therapeutic
access with the husband at the office of Ms. Michelle Hayes?

[
17
]

Both parties agreed during this trial that R. and J. should attend for
counselling with the husband at the office of Ms. Michelle Hayes.  They also
agreed that the sessions shall take place during the husband’s access visits
but they cannot agree on the other terms of the order.

[
18
]

During her closing submissions, the wife took a different position.  She
is not opposed to counselling, but that such counselling should take place in a
“familiar place close to home”.  She submits that the husband should choose a
place that makes the children “comfortable”.  Otherwise, she doubts the
children will try something new.

[
19
]

Although I agree that the children should attend for counselling in an
environment that makes them feel comfortable, there is no evidence to
demonstrate to the Court that they will feel uncomfortable with Ms. Hayes.
Further, Ms. Hayes is located in Hamilton; not far from where J. is attending
school and Oakville where the children live.  Accordingly, I am of the view
that it would be appropriate for the children to attend for therapeutic access with
Ms. Hayes.

[
20
]

The husband would like the
following terms included in the order:

(a)

that the wife fully cooperate and promote counselling with the children;

(b)

that the purpose of the therapy should be for “re-integrating” the
relationship between R. and the husband and to improve the relationship between
J. and the husband; and

(c)

that the fees for the therapy will be paid by the husband but that if it
is determined by the Court that the wife has alienated the children from the
husband, the wife will indemnify the husband for 50% of the counselling costs.

(a)  The Wife’s Cooperation

[
21
]

The wife has advised the Court that she has already told the children
that they will likely be attending therapy with the husband and she is
encouraging them to attend.  I believe the wife when she says that she is
supportive of therapy.  However, even if she was not, I am of the view that it
would not be realistic to include a term in the order that the wife fully
cooperate and support the therapy.  Such an order might simply invite further
court action in the future.  For instance, what is the definition of support
and what standard will the wife be held to if such an order is granted?  If the
husband is of the view that the wife is not supportive, will he bring a motion
in an effort to hold the wife in contempt of my order?  Such a provision is too
vague to be enforceable.  In my view, it is unrealistic to include such a term
in the order and such an order will not be granted.  That being said, I do
expect that the wife will do what she can to encourage the children to attend
the therapy as ordered.

(b)  The Purpose of Therapy

[
22
]

I am also not inclined to make an order that defines the purpose of the therapy.
I presume that Ms. Hayes is qualified to provide the therapeutic access that is
required.  She has both her Bachelors and Masters in social work.  She is also
a Registered Social Worker.  She operates a private practice and she has done
so since August 2002.  She is also a clinical investigator with the Office of
the Children’s Lawyer and has been so since April 2006.  The purpose of the
therapeutic access, as defined by her, is to “strengthen the relationship
between a parent and child”.

[
23
]

I am not going to give Ms. Hayes guidance on how to do her job.  She is
a professional.  I am certain that she will listen to the husband, the wife and
the children and determine what is in their best interests to counsel them
appropriately.  Accordingly, there will be no order defining the purpose of the
therapy.

[
24
]

The wife has also submitted that I should provide guidance in my order
as to what sort of therapy should be provided by Ms. Hayes.  She submitted that
the purpose of the therapy should be “on assisting Mr. G.N. in recognizing the
emotional needs in more adaptive ways, in order to facilitate the reduction of
risk factors, with a view to reintegrating and strengthening their
relationships”.  For the above mentioned reasons, I decline to order any
parameters or restrictions on the therapy to be provided by Ms. Hayes.
However, it would appear that the therapeutic access proposed by Ms. Hayes
may address the issues raised by the wife.

[
25
]

The wife also seeks an order that the therapy will be no more than six
sessions or three months unless the children would like to continue such therapy.
Again, I am not inclined to put time limits on the therapy.  I have heard no
evidence as to how the therapy will proceed or how much time will be required.
Accordingly, I decline to order that the therapy be time limited.

[
26
]

Therapeutic access with the husband and two children will be ordered,
but I will not place any restrictions on what Ms. Hayes is to do.  The wife
will attend the first session with the children.

[
27
]

Despite the agreement between the parties, I am not ordering that the
therapeutic access visits occur solely during the access visits of the
husband.  Although the appointments should ideally be set up during the
husband’s access, it may not always be possible.  If therapeutic access occurs
at a time when the husband is not exercising access, he will be responsible for
transporting the children to and from the scheduled appointments.

(c)  Alienation

[
28
]

The father makes the allegation that the mother has “alienated the
children”.  He claims that the alienation of the two children commenced in June
2003, shortly after the parties physically separated.

I disagree for
the reasons set out below.

Introduction Re:  Alienation

[
29
]

Parental alienation is a disorder that arises most often in child
custody disputes.  Although custody of the children is not an issue in this
proceeding, the husband takes the position that if I should find that the wife
has alienated the children, she should indemnify him for 50% of the therapeutic
access fees payable to Ms. Hayes.

[
30
]

In
C.S. v. M.S.
,
2007 CanLII 6240 (ON SC)
, [2007] O.J. No. 787, 37 R.F.L. (6
th
) 373
(S.C.J. Fam. Ct.) at para.
92
, Perkins J. described parental alienation as
follows:

Children who are subject to the parental alienation syndrome (I
will call them PAS children) are very powerful in their views of the
non-alienating parent. The views are almost exclusively negative, to the point
that the parent is demonized and seen as evil. [...] PAS children feel
empowered and are rewarded for attacking the other parents and feel no remorse
or shame for doing so. [...] PAS children have a knee jerk, reflexive response
to support the alienator against the targeted parent, often on the basis of
minimal evidence or justification. PAS children broaden their attacks to
encompass members of the other parent’s extended family. […] PAS children are
recruited by the alienating parent and alienated siblings to the alienating
parent’s cause. [...] With PAS children, you cannot be sure who you are
listening to ‑ is it the child, is it the alienating parent, or is it
Court Watch [an advocacy group supporting the father]?

[
31
]

In considering the definition of parental alienation provided by Perkins
J. and on the facts before me, I have come to the conclusion that the
allegation of parental alienation has not been made out in this case.

[
32
]

Although the conduct of both parties has not been admirable at all
times, the husband continues to exercise access to his son on a regular basis
and he testified that they have a “fairly good” relationship.  The husband is
not currently exercising access to his daughter on a regular basis because
he

decided to end their visits in August 2009. He felt that she was disrespectful
to him during an argument.  Although there may be times where the relationship
between the husband and the children is strained, there is no evidence that
either R. or J. have views of their father which are almost exclusively
negative as a result of parental alienation.

[
33
]

The father submits that the alienation is “profound” and it has its
basis in the following acts:

(a)

that the husband did not see his children for many weeks after he left
the matrimonial home on June 20, 2003;

(b)

that the wife and the children moved to Oakville from Toronto in
August/September 2003 in an effort to make access difficult for the husband;

(c)

that the wife seized the husband’s motor vehicle in September 2003 to
make access to the children impossible;

(d)

that the wife contacted Jewish Family & Child Services regarding
allegations against the husband;

(e)

that the wife reported incidents to the Halton CAS in an effort to
alienate the children from their father;

(f)

that the wife enrolled the children in “Safety Zone” counselling;

(g)

that the wife called the police on five separate occasions making
allegations against the husband;

(h)

that the wife blamed the fact that their daughter R. could not go to the
school of her choice on September 2009 on the husband;

(i)

the children do not always use the surname “N.”;

(j)

other acts of alienation regarding access, particularly on holidays; and

(k)

that the wife threatened to cancel J.’s attendance at Cadets.

[
34
]

I will now deal with each of these allegations separately.

a.

No access schedule after separating on June 20, 2003

[
35
]

The parties physically separated on June 20, 2003 following an assault
in the home.  Both parties were charged criminally.  The wife and the husband
were released on promises to appear.  The terms of the husband’s promise to
appear included that he was to “abstain from communicating, directly or
indirectly, with L.N.” (the wife).  There was no exception to allow the parties
to communicate for the purpose of exercising access to the children.  Although
the documentation was not placed before me, it appears that the husband pleaded
guilty to the assault charge and he was put on probation.  There is no evidence
before me as to when that plea occurred.

[
36
]

At some point the husband was charged with failing to comply with his
probation because he had violated a non-communication order with the wife.
There was a trial following which the husband was found guilty.  He received a
suspended sentence on January 13, 2006 and he was put on probation for 12
months during which time he was to keep the peace and be of good behaviour,
etc.  There was no order which prevented communication between the parties.

[
37
]

In an effort to arrange custody shortly after June 20, 2003 and because
of the non-communication order, the parties accepted the mediation services of
a friend, Ms. A.W..  Ms. A.W. was to facilitate the husband’s access to the
children.  The first access visit was arranged for June 27, 2003 but the wife
could not fulfill that commitment.

[
38
]

Because the access visit was frustrated on June 27, 2003, a visit was
proposed by the husband on June 28, 2003 with an overnight to June 29, 2003 so
that he could take the children to church.  The wife agreed to such a visit.

[
39
]

The husband also proposed that he take the children on Wednesday, July
2, 2003 “weather permitting”, or the next day.  He planned to take the children
to Ontario Place for the day.  The wife responded that she was “not available
for Wednesday, […], 2003 …Thursday, […], 2003 (J.’s birthday) is better”.

[
40
]

The husband confirmed that he would be taking the children on […], 2003
to Ontario Place but that he would like to pick them up at 4:30 p.m. on
Wednesday, […], 2003 and return them on Thursday, […], 2003 at 7:30 or 8:00
p.m.  As of 2:30 p.m. on […], 2003 the wife had still not confirmed the pick up
time.  It appears that a discussion took place between Ms. A.W. and the husband
thereafter.  Ms. A.W. then wrote an e-mail to the husband stating: “your
arrangements to pick up your children at 4:30 p.m. today has [sic] been
terminated as per
your request
”.  [Emphasis added]  Thereafter, the
husband terminated Ms. A.W. as the mediator for purposes of exercising access.

[
41
]

The next person who tried to assist the parties in exercising access was
their pastor, Pastor Klink.   Pastor Klink attempted to provide counselling to
the parties rather than to simply facilitate access.  This was not agreeable to
the wife and as a result, his role as “mediator” for the parties was
terminated.

[
42
]

The husband then retained the services of Mr. Jerry Herszkopf, barrister
and solicitor.  He wrote to the wife on July 9, 2003 and suggested that the
husband have immediate access to the children. The issue of alienation arose
for the first time in this letter despite the fact that the parties had only
been separated for approximately 19 days.  Mr. Herszkopf stated that it is
“imperative that the children have access to their father on a timetable to be
agreed upon.  It is definitely not in the best interest to alienate the
children from their father even though the two of you are having a dispute”.

[
43
]

The wife responded to Mr. Herszkopf’s letter on July 15, 2003.  She
advised Mr. Herszkopf that she had never denied the husband access and
that she had been waiting to hear from him since he cancelled the last visit
and fired the mediator. She also advised that she was looking forward to
hearing from the husband soon regarding the children’s next visit as “they were
disappointed that he cancelled their last visit, as they were looking forward
to going to Ontario Place on J.’s birthday”.

[
44
]

The wife then wrote about access going forward.  She said:

“I would like to set up consistent visitation times that will
be the same every week for the sake of the children.  It has been suggested to
me that the norm for visitation is every Wednesday evening (for dinner) until
about 8:00 p.m. and every other weekend.  The place of dropping off and picking
up will be agreed upon now and will always be the same, for consistency and
predictability.”

[
45
]

It was agreed that the husband would have overnight access three days
later and on Friday, July 18, 2003.  The husband testified that he saw the
children next in August 2003; however, he was not satisfied with the
consistency of the visits.  Despite his dissatisfaction, there was no evidence
before the Court of a response to the proposed schedule made by the wife on
July 15, 2003.

[
46
]

The husband served an emergency notice of motion on August 29, 2003
which was returnable September 9, 2003.  At the return of the motion, and without
the presence of the wife although duly served, Herman Siegel J. ordered that
the husband have access to the children on four occasions, including overnight
visits from September 12, 2003 to September 20, 2003.

[
47
]

Although the husband was not satisfied with the access arrangements from
June 20, 2003 to September 9, 2003, the above mentioned correspondence shows
that the wife was not intentionally trying to frustrate such access.  I accept
her evidence and the content of the correspondence that demonstrates she was
trying to facilitate access.  Her evidence is supported by the fact that she
granted overnight access to the husband within a week of separation and she
tried to accommodate him for J.’s birthday.  The wife also made a proposal for
a schedule of access within 25 days of separation (on July 15, 2003), offering
weekend access every other weekend and one mid-week access which is almost similar
to what the husband is exercising now.

[
48
]

In my view, if the husband was really interested in seeing the children
as he professes, he would have accepted the proposal made by the wife on July
15, 2003.  If, after having tried this routine, he wanted greater access he
should have asked for it.  If his proposal for greater access was declined,
then it would have been appropriate for the husband to bring a motion before
the court seeking this relief.  This is not what he did.  He sought relief from
the court without even trying the proposal as set out by the wife.

[
49
]

It is obvious that the arrangements for the husband to see the children
were not ideal following separation.  The use of a third party to facilitate
access was not perfect but there was no other choice at the time – the husband
was subject to a non-communication order with the wife.  Scheduling access when
the parties can communicate is difficult.  The difficulty is further compounded
when there is a non-communication order in place.  That being said, the parties
should make every effort to do what is in the best interests of the children
and in my view, the wife tried to do just that.  The husband was not so
cooperative and the allegation that the wife was alienating the children
through her conduct immediately following separation has no foundation.

b.

The move to Oakville

[
50
]

The husband submits that the move to Oakville from Toronto was a
calculated move by the wife to make access difficult for the husband, thereby
alienating the children.  In my view, the move to Oakville was not done for
this purpose although it would have made travel for the husband to exercise access
more cumbersome.

[
51
]

I accept the explanation given by the wife for the move to Oakville.  She testified that she had started a Lice Squad business with the husband.  The
area that the business was to cover was Oakville, Burlington and Hamilton.  The wife testified that prior to separation, she had told the husband that she
would like to move to the Oakville area so she could be more “hands on” in the
business.  I accept her evidence in this regard.

[
52
]

The husband suggested that the wife’s intent to move to Oakville to be more involved in the community where the business was to operate is
disingenuous.  He pointed to an e-mail from Ms. Dawn Mucci, dated March 4, 2003,
that showed it was possible to hire lice pickers to work for the business and
remain in Toronto.  The wife agreed that that was true, but she felt it would
be better for her to live in the area so that she could be more involved in the
marketing of the business and be closer to her workers and potential clients.
I accept such an explanation.

[
53
]

The husband also submitted that the fact they signed a three-year lease
for their rental property on Brightwood Avenue in Toronto in January 2003 shows
that there was no intention, at that time, to move to the Oakville area.  The
wife testified, and I accept her evidence, that she planned to start the Lice
Squad business and work from Toronto in the interim.  She told the husband that
she wanted to move to Oakville and that signing the lease for three years for a
home in Toronto was not appropriate.  She was advised by the husband that the
rent was cheap for Toronto, they could break the lease and/or they could sublet
it to tenants and earn a profit from it.  I accept the wife’s evidence in this
regard ‑ that signing a three-year lease on a property in Toronto did not preclude any intention by the parties, specifically the wife, to move to
the Oakville area.

[
54
]

The wife was also cross-examined on the fact that she had sworn an
affidavit stating that living in Oakville was preferable to living in Toronto because the schools were closer.  The husband submitted Mapquest directions and
estimated travel times from the home in Toronto to the school in Toronto and
the home in Oakville to the school in Oakville.  It appears that the physical
distance between the home in Oakville and the school in Oakville was double
that of Toronto.  However, when asked about the difference in driving times,
the wife testified that the time it took her to drive that distance in Oakville was less than her travel time in Toronto.  I accept the wife’s testimony in that
regard.

[
55
]

Notwithstanding the fact that I accept the wife’s evidence of the
reasons for the move to Oakville, I do find the fact that the wife did not
advise the husband of her move until after it was done, somewhat troubling.  It
appears that the husband only became aware of such a move after he attended a
motion before the Court on September 9, 2003 wherein Herman Siegal J. ordered
that the wife be precluded from moving within 5 kms. of the home in Toronto.  It was at that point or shortly thereafter that the husband was advised of the
move.

[
56
]

The husband has a right to know where his children are living and that
right exists regardless of the troubles between the parties.  That being said,
I am of view that although the wife’s move to Oakville would have made access a
little more difficult to exercise, it was not her intent to move to Oakville to frustrate the husband’s access and for the purpose of alienating the children
from their father.  If she intended her move for that purpose, presumably she
would have moved further than Oakville and perhaps to Northern Ontario where
her family lives.

c.

Seizure of the car

[
57
]

As of the date of separation, there were two vehicles that were
available to the parties.  One was a van and the other was a Nissan Maxima
sedan.  Both of the vehicles were registered in the name of the wife.  When the
parties separated, the wife kept the van and the husband took the sedan.  The
husband maintained insurance on both vehicles following separation.

[
58
]

Approximately three months after the parties separated, the wife
attended with the police to seize the sedan.  The reason given by the wife for
the seizure of the sedan was that she was worried that the sedan was not
properly insured and that the husband had a bad driving record.  I do not
accept either of these reasons.

[
59
]

It appears from the records produced at this trial that the sedan was
always properly insured and that the insurance paid for the sedan was not
extraordinary.  The insurance paid for the van and the sedan was approximately
the same.  Presuming the insurer was aware that the husband was driving the
sedan, I would have expected the insurance of for it to be much greater than
the insurance for the van because of the husband’s bad driving record, if it
existed.  That was not the case.

[
60
]

The issue of insurance could have easily been resolved by the wife if
she had simply written to counsel for the husband to confirm that there was
insurance on the sedan.  The wife did not do so and I am of the view that there
is no merit to the wife’s allegation that the husband had a bad driving record.

[
61
]

Although I am extremely troubled by the wife seizing the sedan, I am not
of the view that it was solely for the purpose of making access difficult, if
not impossible for the husband and therefore alienating the children.  There is
no evidence before this Court that the children knew of the seizure of the
van.  I believe that the sedan was seized by the wife out of spite for the
husband as opposed to any attempt to alienate the children.

d.

Contacting Jewish Family and Child Services

[
62
]

The husband submits that the wife involved Jewish and Family Services (“JF
& CS”) with their family in an effort to alienate the children.  The wife
testified that she only involved JF & CS in order to protect the children.

[
63
]

JF & CS was involved with the parties as early as September, 2001 –
well before the parties separated.  There were problems regarding their son, A..
He was assaulting his sister R.; threatening his mother and had thoughts of
committing suicide.  He was ultimately removed from the home on March 12,
2003.

[
64
]

The history involving A. is not entirely relevant to this issue but
there was a call made by the wife to JF & CS on April 21, 2005 which is
relevant.  The wife alleged that the husband yelled at the children and
threatened to spank them during his access visits making them feel afraid.  JF
& CS confirmed that this occurred when they interviewed J. and R..  The
report also states that:  “During interview with father, he did admit to yelling
and making threats to spank and stated sometimes he gets very frustrated with
their behaviour.  He assured worker that he would attempt to be more
appropriate”.

[
65
]

It appears from the JF & CS report of May 2, 2005 that the concerns
raised by the wife regarding the children were confirmed by both the children
and the husband.  It was also concluded by JF & CS that:  “This worker had
to put an immediate safety intervention plan into place prior to the visit, in
getting father’s assurance that he would be appropriate”.

[
66
]

In light of the investigation and conclusions made by JF & CS on
this date, it does not appear that the wife called it to make false allegations
against the husband.  Her allegations were confirmed, the husband agreed that
he had acted inappropriately and he assured JF & CS that he would be more
appropriate with the children.  It is my view that the wife took appropriate
steps in protecting her children in this instance and the wife did not involve
JF & CS for the purpose of alienating the children.

e.

Contacting the Halton Children’s Aid Society

[
67
]

The husband submits that the wife involved the CAS for the sole purpose
of alienating the children.  The CAS was contacted on four separate occasions
by the wife.  I will deal with each incident individually.

#1:
November 29, 2005

[
68
]

On November 29, 2005, the CAS opened a file regarding the N. family.  On
that day, the wife reported a number of allegations of abuse regarding the
husband.

[
69
]

Amongst other things, the wife alleged that the husband hit R. on the leg
very hard after she spilled ketchup in his car.  It was also alleged that J.
was hit on the head by the husband.  She also advised CAS that a month prior, R.
had reported that while they were at the library, she scared J. by sneaking up
on him.  They engaged in a game of chase in the library and the husband caught R..
The husband held R.’s arms down and told J. to kick her and then laughed.  R.
ended up kicking the husband and J..  Both children were upset and when J. came
home, he went to his room and cried.

[
70
]

The husband was interviewed by the CAS and he reported that he had held R.
twice and asked her how she would feel if her brother hit her.  He admitted
that he hit J. on the head with a foam sandal and that he did slap R.’s leg
when she spilled ketchup in the van.  He also reported that when the children
normally were in trouble, he used “
consequences
and never hit them with
implements”. [Emphasis added]

[
71
]

The children confirmed the incidents described above but R. added that
when the husband held her for J. to hit her, it was not done in a playful
manner and that she was scared.  The children also added that the husband used
physical discipline.

[
72
]

At the conclusion of the investigation, the allegations were not
“verified”; however, the husband was cautioned with respect to the use of
physical discipline and he was made aware of the possible consequences.  The
husband “accepted” the caution and as a result the matter was closed on January
12, 2006.

[
73
]

In light of the fact that the allegations of the wife were confirmed by
the children and the husband, I cannot accept the submission by the husband
that the purpose of calling the CAS on this occasion was to alienate the
children.  Surely the wife cannot be criticized for taking the appropriate
steps to protect her children.  I am of the view that the wife acted entirely
appropriately in these circumstances.

[
74
]

It was suggested in cross-examination of the wife that she was further
alienating the children because she did not tell the children that the father
had been “cleared” following the CAS involvement on this occasion.  He was not
cleared.  The report states that “the protection concerns of caregiver capacity
and physical discipline were not verified.”  However, the husband was cautioned
and he accepted such a caution.  For the wife to tell the children that their
father was “cleared” by the CAS would have been untruthful and I do not
consider her conduct in this regard to have contributed to the alienation of
the children.

#2:  March
6, 2006

[
75
]

The CAS conducted a second investigation as a result of a call from the
wife on March 6, 2006.  She reported that J. had two scabs on his back which
looked like finger nail marks surrounded by a bruise.  There was also a bruise
on J.’s hip that was in the shape of a thumb print.  These marks were noticed
upon his return from a visit with the husband.  J. said he did not know how he
got the marks and he was “protective” of his father.

[
76
]

When interviewed by the CAS, J. said that he had wrestled with his
father, that he did not know where the bruises came from, that his father had
not physically disciplined him during the visit and that “he was not afraid of
[the husband] and felt comfortable in [the husband’s] home”.

[
77
]

Upon investigation of this matter, “the concern of physical discipline
was not verified”.  Further, the CAS advised the wife that “unless the child
disclosed or made an allegation, she should not contact the Society”.  They
also concluded that:  “…it appeared that the allegations were more malicious
rather than suspicions of abuse”.

[
78
]

I accept the findings of the CAS that the allegations made by the wife
in this particular case were unfounded.  That being said, I do not accept that
this report to the CAS, in and of itself, supports an allegation of parental
alienation by the wife.

[
79
]

Although it may not have been prudent for the wife to have called CAS on
this occasion, the facts of this incident do not support an allegation of
parental alienation.  The wife, herself, said that J. was very “protective” of
his father.  Further, J. told the CAS that he was not “afraid” of his father
and felt “comfortable” in his home.  This shows that J., as of March 2006, had
a positive view of his father and not a negative one.  The comments also
demonstrate that J. was not supporting the alienator (the wife) against the
targeted parent (the husband).  If the wife was alienating J. against the
father at this time, she was not doing a very good job of it.

#3:  May
11, 2006

[
80
]

On May 11, 2003, a “third party” reported that the wife had told her that
while play wrestling with J., the husband slipped his hand under J.’s underwear
and said:  “what’s down here?”  R., who was present, slapped the husband on the
wrist and told him to stop.  Further, J. told an inappropriate joke and the
husband slapped him on the back of the head four times.  Neither J. nor the
husband verified the allegations raised with the CAS but R. did confirm the
allegation about the wrestling incident.

[
81
]

The “third party” was not identified in the CAS report but the wife
testified that the third party was her counsellor, Laurie.  The wife testified
that when she heard about the allegations, she did not know what to do as she
had been cautioned about calling the CAS.  As a result of the disclosure to her
counsellor, her counsellor reported the allegations, not the wife.  The wife
was not interviewed as part of this investigation.  I accept this evidence.

[
82
]

Despite the fact that the CAS did not verify protection concerns of
inappropriate discipline or abusive sexual activity, they felt obligated to
caution both parents about discipline and the husband about respecting personal
space.  Accordingly, the involvement of the CAS in these circumstances was not
completely without merit.

[
83
]

Further, I am of the view that the wife acted entirely appropriately in
speaking to her counsellor about the allegations.  She testified that she did
not know what to do when she heard the allegations.  She did not simply pick up
the phone and call either the CAS or the police when she was advised of the
circumstances.  She went to her counsellor and discussed the issues.  It was
the counsellor who contacted the CAS.  There was no suggestion that the wife
told the counsellor to report the incident.  Accordingly, I do not accept the
submission that the contact with the CAS on this occasion was made in an effort
to alienate the children.

#4:       April
5, 2007

[
84
]

On April 5, 2007, the wife reported to the CAS that the children had
returned from a March break vacation.  The husband, the children and third
parties were in a hotel room together.  The husband slept with one of the
children and he slept naked.  When he got out of bed, he asked the children to
turn their heads.  The wife also reported that the husband took a swing at a
child who ducked.  She also reported that J. was “terrified” of the husband.

[
85
]

The husband and J. denied the allegations, but R. advised that the
husband took a swing at J.’s head and he ducked.  She also advised that the
husband wore only a t-shirt to bed and put something on when he got up.  The husband
advised R. that he was not wearing underwear and to look the other way.

[
86
]

The husband accepted the CAS’s advice to have separate rooms from R. and
the third party.  The husband was also cautioned about using inappropriate
discipline with J..  In light of the fact that R. confirmed the allegations
reported by the wife and the CAS felt compelled to caution the husband, I am of
the view that reporting this particular incident to the CAS was not done in an
effort to alienate the children.

[
87
]

That being said, I do have some concerns about the conduct of the wife
that arose as a result of the CAS investigation in April, 2007.  During this
investigation J. advised that there were times that he felt depressed and at
those times he did not want to speak to anyone.  It had nothing to do with the
husband, but when he returned from an access visit, he did not want to be
spoken to.  He would “cry, feel mad, and had thoughts of suicide”.  It was
reported that “his mother and a third party encouraged him to talk when he returned
from visiting [the husband], and at those times he felt low and he yelled at
his mother and the third party to ‘go away’”.  The wife admitted that she did
question the children about their time spent with the husband upon their return
from access visits with him.

[
88
]

As a result of the wife’s conduct, protection concerns with respect to
the emotional harm inflicted were verified against her.  The CAS cautioned the
wife not to ask questions about the children’s activities with the husband and
to let the children approach her with any information.  The wife agreed to
amend her questioning of the children.

[
89
]

It is not clear how long the questioning of the children regarding their
access visits with the husband occurred.  However, it is clear that any questioning
of any child following a visit is inappropriate.  That being said, I cannot
find that such questioning led to any alienation of the father.  In fact, the
opposite occurred.  J. complained about the conduct of the mother to the CAS
during this investigation.  This complaint by J. flies completely in the face
of the theory that the husband was being alienated by the mother through her
conduct with the children.  If the alienation had been working, J. would have
supported his mother and the allegations made against the husband.  That was
not the case.  Accordingly, I do not find that the call to the CAS on this
occasion was for the purpose of alienating the children.

f.

Safety Zone Counselling

[
90
]

The husband submits that the children’s participation in counselling at
“Safety Zone” was totally inappropriate and a “dramatic” attempt by the wife to
alienate the children from their father.  I totally disagree.

[
91
]

It appears that the children were enrolled in the Safety Zone program
from September to December, 2005.  The wife testified that the children
completed the counseling and that they enjoyed it.  I accept that evidence.

[
92
]

The Safety Zone brochure was provided as an exhibit in these
proceedings.   It describes the program and states that the program provides
children and their mothers with safe, nurturing environments in which they can
“discuss the violence and abuse they have experienced” amongst other things.
Further, it states that “the program supports children to heal from the effects
of exposure to woman abuse and supports mothers to assist their children in
this healing procedure”.

[
93
]

The children’s group discusses topics such as:  “anger and resolving
conflicts”; “personal safety”; “responsibility for violence”; “self esteem” and
“family changes”.

[
94
]

The husband seems to take issue with the Safety Zone because he believes
that it is “anti father” or “anti husband”.  He submits that it simply
reinforces the idea that the wife and children have been abused by him.

[
95
]

Despite the submissions of the husband, the reality is that the children
did experience abuse in the home.  In January 2002 A. (then 13 years old) was
apprehended under the
Mental Health Act
[1]

because he attacked his mother.  He threatened to kill her, went after her with
a knife, hit her with a baseball bat and spat at her.  The police were called
to the home and calmed A. down.  The JF & CS report states that “Parents
are concerned for their own safety and safety of other children in the home
ages 4 and 7”.

[
96
]

The JF & CS were also involved
immediately after the parties were separated in June 2003 following an
altercation in the home.  The introduction to the report states that “At issue
here is
witnessing of the children
but that is not an immediate concern
as the situation is now calm and significantly changed with the couple living
separately”.  [Emphasis added]

[
97
]

The report also states:  “R.
witnessed the physical altercation between her parents and called police.  J.
did not see anything except the broken furniture after the event.  He did hear
the yelling and saw the police arrive”.  The husband testified that what he
regrets most about this incident is that his daughter witnessed the assault and
that she was involved in it by calling 911.  The husband ultimately plead
guilty to assault arising from this incident for which he received a
conditional discharge.

[
98
]

Further, the husband admitted that
during the summer of 2005, he had hit J. on the head with a sandal and that he
had slapped R.’s leg when she spilled ketchup in the van.

[
99
]

In light of the incidents described
above, I believe that it was perfectly reasonable for the wife to enrol the
children in the Safety Zone counselling.  They had witnessed violence in the
home and experienced it themselves.  Surely, it was entirely appropriate for
them to attend at a facility where they felt comfortable.

[
100
]

There is absolutely no evidence before this court to show that the
children were “indoctrinated” into believing that they (or their mother) were
the victims of abuse by their father.  On the contrary, the violence that was
witnessed by the children (and admitted to by the husband) occurred long before
counselling began.

[
101
]

There was no “indoctrination” such that the children believed they were
victims of abuse and therefore the relationship with their father was strained.
In fact, the opposite occurred.  J. reported to the CAS on March 6, 2006, three
months after he had completed the counselling, that “he was not afraid” of the
husband and felt “comfortable in [his] home”.  He advised the CAS in and around
May 11, 2006 that there was no physical violence in the husband’s home.  In
fact, he said that “a year ago [prior to the counselling commencing], [the
husband] hit [him] but now you held his neck and turned his head towards [the
husband]”.

[
102
]

The same can be said for R..  She was not convinced, through
counselling, that her father was abusive.  In and around April 2007, R.
reported that:  “no one used physical discipline with her or J. and then she
stated that physical discipline was not used as usual discipline”.  There was
no attempt, whatsoever, by R. to paint her father as an abuser which had its
foundation in the counselling she attended almost two years prior.

[
103
]

Further, the husband was invited to participate in counselling with the
children.  Immediately after the husband found out that the children were
enrolled in counselling at the Safety Zone on March 22, 2006, the wife advised
that there was counselling at Halton Family Services for parents dealing with
separation.  She also advised that the children “loved” the group sessions at
the Safety Zone and that the wife would like to register them again.  The
husband was invited to participate.

[
104
]

It does not appear that the husband decided to participate.  Rather than
accept the offer, he brought another motion regarding the counselling issue
before Jarvis J. in June, 2006.  The husband felt that Horkins J. was
misinformed on the counselling issue during the motion of March 22, 2006 and he
sought to re-litigate it.  Jarvis J. held:  “I am satisfied that he [the
husband] has chosen not to avail himself of the Halton Services available to
him and that he has totally misconceived that agency’s continued involvement in
his children’s interests”.  No change in counselling was ordered.

[
105
]

If the husband was so concerned that the Safety Zone counselling was a
design by the wife to alienate the children from him, I am uncertain as to why
the wife would ask him to participate in the counselling so that he could
learn, first hand, of her strategy.  I am also unclear as to why the husband would
not participate in such counselling to determine the exact nature of the
counselling and to make the submission of alienation from a position of
knowledge rather than a simple allegation.  In my view, the wife enrolled the
children in the Safety Zone counselling for a proper reason and not for the
purpose of alienating the children.

g.

Contacting the Police

[
106
]

The husband alleges that the wife contacted the police on five separate
occasions which was unwarranted.  The husband submits that such contact was designed
to alienate the children.  I do not agree.  I will deal with each occurrence
separately.

#1:  The
Nissan Incident

[
107
]

The husband alleges that the wife called the police to assist in
retrieving the Nissan Maxima sedan and that that was done in order to alienate
the children.  I have already stated that I am of the view that the
repossessing of the sedan was not appropriate.  However, I do not accept that
such an incident is a factor to be considered in the analysis of alienation.

[
108
]

There is no evidence, whatsoever, that the children witnessed or even
knew that the police were called in this incident.  Accordingly, I cannot say
that the police involvement on this occasion was designed to alienate the
children.

#2:  The
Deerhurst Inn Incident

[
109
]

The husband testified that during the March break in 2005, he took the
children to the Deerhurst Inn, outside of Huntsville.  He believed that he was
to have the children returned to he wife on the Wednesday of that week.  The
wife testified that the children were to be returned home on Tuesday.

[
110
]

While the husband was having dinner with the children on the Tuesday
night, he received a call from a police officer.  The police officer told him
that the wife had told them that she had custody of the children and that they were
to be returned on Tuesday.  The husband was told, during this conversation,
that the children were to be returned by Wednesday at 5 p.m.

[
111
]

The wife testified that she called the police on the Tuesday of the
March break because she had called the husband a number of times but got no
response.  As a result, she involved the police to contact the husband and have
the children returned home.

[
112
]

It appears that all of the contact between the police and the husband
was on the phone and there was no personal contact between the police and the
children.  There was no evidence,, whatsoever that the children knew of this
call.  In light of this, I do not attribute the motive of the wife calling the
police in this circumstance was for the purpose of alienating the children.

[
113
]

Although I accept the explanation of the wife for calling the police on
this occasion, I question the utility of involving the police force in such a
family matter.  There had been numerous times that the husband returned the
children late.  There had never been any allegation that the husband was going
to kidnap the children, etc.  Further, I did not hear the wife say that she was
concerned about the welfare of the children on this occasion, she just got no
response from the husband when she called him.

[
114
]

Despite the fact that I do not approve of the wife’s conduct of calling
the police in these circumstances, I do not conclude that her motive in calling
the police was to alienate the children.

#3:  The
Elim Lodge Incident

[
115
]

The wife called the police after the husband and children had been on
vacation at Elim Lodge in the summer of 2005.  The wife picked the children up
at the home of the husband’s mother after this vacation.  The wife testified
that as the children approached the van, they appeared to be upset.  J.
reported that the husband had hit him on the head with a sandal.  R. reported
that her father had hit her so hard on her leg that it left an imprint.  She
also said that if the husband had done this to J., he would have “broken
down”.  The police were called following this disclosure.

[
116
]

The police attended and spoke with wife, at the very least.  There was
no evidence before me that the children were interviewed.  There were no
criminal charges laid against the husband arising out of this incident.

[
117
]

It does not appear to me that the police were called on this occasion in
order to alienate the children.  As I have stated above, the CAS confirmed that
J. had been hit on the head and that R. had been slapped.  The husband was
cautioned about the use of such discipline and he accepted such a caution.  The
husband could have been charged with a criminal offence arising out of the two
incidents which he admitted.  It is unfortunate to have involved the police but
it appears that the wife had concerns which were borne out following the CAS
investigation.  It was not a false allegation even though charges were not
laid.

#4:
September 2005

[
118
]

The husband submits that the wife called the police in September 2005 in
a further attempt to alienate the children.  The police were called at this
time because J. was crying in his room.

[
119
]

It does not appear to me that the police were called on this occasion to
alienate the children against the husband.  The police were called on this
occasion because the wife had concerns about J.’s well being.  I accept the
wife’s evidence in this regard.

#5:       Niagara
Falls:  December 2005

[
120
]

The last incident where the police were called was when the husband took
the children to Niagara Falls during their Christmas holidays in December 2005.
It had been determined that the parents would equally share the Christmas
holidays that year.

[
121
]

It is clear that the Christmas holiday was for a period of 15 days (December
20, 2005 to January 4, 2006).  There was a handwritten note made by the wife suggesting
that the husband could have the children from December 20 to 21, 2005 (one day)
and then from December 25 at 3:00 p.m. to December 29 at 5:00 p.m. (four
days).  The husband was not satisfied with such a proposal because five days
represented only one-third of the Christmas vacation as opposed to one-half.

[
122
]

I did not see any correspondence or hear any evidence about any
corresponding proposal from the husband for Christmas access.  For instance,
there was no fax filed before this Court from the husband to the wife
suggesting that her proposed access was not agreeable and that the husband
wanted more days with the children.

[
123
]

The husband testified that he took the two children and a friend of R.’s
to Niagara Falls where there was a water park.  When they were in Niagara Falls, the husband called the wife and told her that he was going to keep the
children for an extra day.  He did not advise the children that he was going to
do such a thing.  The husband described the wife as furious and “she pretty much”
said that he was going to “pay”.

[
124
]

Following the telephone conversation with the wife regarding the extra
day in Niagara Falls, the husband got a call from the police.  He advised the
police that he had access to the children and that he was going to return the
children to the wife the following day, which he did.

[
125
]

Again, I cannot accept that the call to the police on this occasion
resulted in alienation of the children.  There was no attendance by the police
to speak to the husband in person during the trip to Niagara Falls.  The
contact from the police was by phone.   There was no evidence before this Court
for me to conclude that the children were advised or even knew of the police
telephone call, resulting in some form of alienation.

[
126
]

I might add that it is unfortunate that the wife decided to call the
police in the circumstances of the children being in Niagara Falls with their
father.  There was no indication, at that time, that the children were in
peril.  For instance, there was no telephone call to the wife from the children
suggesting that they were in jeopardy or that they wanted to come home.  That
being said, I do not believe that the call was made to alienate the children.
I believe that the call was made out of the wife’s frustration in the husband
not returning the children in a timely manner.

[
127
]

I do not believe that any of the calls to the police were made for the
purpose of alienating the children.  I do not know if the children were aware
of the calls and even if they were, I heard no expert evidence about the
effects of police involvement in this case.  As such, I dismiss the telephone
calls to the police as a factor in the wife trying to alienate the children.

h.

R.’s schooling issue

[
128
]

In May 2009, R. expressed to her father that she had an interest in
attending a private school by the name of King’s Christian Collegiate.  As a
result, the husband wrote to the wife.  He confirmed that he would pay half of
all expenses but that “it can only occur if you are solely enrolling her
because you show no income.  I will call on your behalf and negotiate the best
possible tuition and will then forward the total cost to you.  You can then
decide based on my paying half whether you are willing to go ahead”.  Such a
representation to the school that the wife was solely responsible for enrolling
R. would be false because it was anticipated that each parent would pay half of
the tuition.

[
129
]

The wife did not make any representations to the school regarding
payment and there were many fax exchanges between the parties regarding payment
of expenses for R.’s schooling.  The upshot was that the wife was only able to
contribute $2,000 for all of the expenses of R.’s schooling.  The husband
responded saying that unless the wife could contribute more than $2,000, R. attending
her school of choice was not possible.

[
130
]

Despite this fax exchange, it appears that the parties were continuing
to make efforts to raise the money to send R. to the school of her choice.  The
application was made for R. to attend the school but there was no commitment as
to how the fees were going to be paid.

[
131
]

In the interim, the wife was able to obtain a bursary in the amount of
$3,000 to reduce the fees but she did not advise the husband.  Accordingly, she
would reap the benefit of the bursary on her side of the ledger but the husband
would not.  The husband expected to share the fees of the school equally but to
also benefit from any reduction in fees, equally.  The wife seemed to take the
position that because she obtained the bursary, only she should benefit from
it.  Such conduct was not admirable as it appeared that both parties were
making efforts to send R. to the private school.

[
132
]

Thereafter, the wife’s child support and tax credit were greatly reduced
and on August 13, 2009 she advised the husband that she was not in a position
to send R. to King’s Christian Collegiate.  In her fax she said that this has
made R. “very disappointed”.  Nowhere in this fax does she blame the husband
for the inability to send R. to school but suggests that if the husband wishes
to “contribute further to their education, that is up to you [the husband]”.

[
133
]

The content of the fax sent to the husband on August 13, 2009 is
consistent with the evidence given by the wife during this trial.  She said
that she told R. that it was neither her fault nor the husband’s fault that R.
could not attend King’s Christian Collegiate in the fall of 2009.

[
134
]

The wife testified that R. was upset because the parties could not
afford to send her to private school.  The wife did not blame the husband and
she did not tell R. to call the father and blame him.  I accept this evidence.

[
135
]

During the time that the parents were trying to raise the funds and in
August, 2009, R. did call the husband.  She told the husband that her mother

Conclusion Regarding Alienation

[
164
]

The husband asks me to rely on the case of
A.G.L. v. K.B.D.

(2009),
2009 CanLII 943 (ON SC)
, 65 R.F.L. (6th) 146 (Ont. S.C.J.) to find that the wife has alienated
the children.  That case can be easily distinguished from the case before me.
In that particular case, the applicant alleged that the alienation began from
the time each of his three children were born and continued to the present
day.  Such is not the case before me. The husband has had access to the
children since separation and he continues to see them for access visits up
until the present.  As I have outlined above, the wife has attempted to
facilitate access rather than frustrate it .

[
165
]

Dr. Barbara Fidler testified in the case of
A.G.L. v. K.B.C.
,
supra
.
She was qualified as an expert in areas of clinical psychology, custody and
access assessments and high conflict custody disputes, including parental
alienation cases.  Dr. Fidler gave an assessment dated February 10, 2000 and in
it she concluded that the children faced a “serious risk of aligning with
K.D.

[the respondent, mother] and being alienated from
A.L.
[the applicant,
father]”.  Dr. Fiddler’s report was eight years old at the time of trial but McWatt J.
concluded that not much had changed since it was produced.  She accepted the
evidence of Dr. Fidler and she concluded that “the children have aged and Dr.
Fidler’s predictions and fears have, in fact been realized” and that “K.D. has
conducted a consistent an overwhelming campaign, for more than a decade, to
alienate A.L.’s three children from him”.  I did not make similar findings
based upon the evidence presented to me.

[
166
]

There was no report filed in the case before me and no expert witness
testified about parental alienation.  The husband asks me to rely on a table
that was referred to in the case of
A.G.L. v. K.B.D.
,
supra
at
para.
92
.  It is entitled: “Pathological Alienation:  Warning Signs of
Behaviours Exhibited by Child, Alienating Parent & Rejected Parent”.  There
are 60 bullet points in this table outlining the warning signs to look for to
determine whether parental alienation exits.  In my view, the evidence at this
trial satisfies only one or two of the warning signs.   Those warning signs are
that the wife engaged in inquisition of the child (J.) after visits with the
husband and sometimes adhered to the wishes of the children when they did not
want to see their father.

[
167
]

For the reasons set out above, I do not find that the wife has alienated
the children whatsoever pursuant to the definition set out by Perkins J. in
C.S. v. M.S. (supra) or otherwise..  As such, she will not be required to
reimburse the husband for any costs associated with therapeutic access.

3.         Should
there be an order prohibiting the wife from using the children as
“go-betweens”?

[
168
]

The husband seeks an order that both parents be prohibited:

“.… from using the children as messengers or go-betweens with
regard to (i) inflammatory issues; (ii) issues or factual contentions that are
in dispute between G.N. and L.N. [the parties]; (iii) any communication, which
if received or heard by the child, would not be well received by the child.”

[
169
]

The husband also seeks an order directing each parent to:

“… tell the children that at any time a message is communicated
that when the other parent says, ‘I need to discuss it with mom/dad’ the child
is to immediately cease any further communication regarding that matter.”

[
170
]

Orders cannot be unclear and ambiguous.  As the Quebec Court of Appeal
has ruled:  “… the order must be precise, for the persons against whom it is
issued must know exactly what they can do and what they must absolutely refrain
from doing.  There is little room for interpretation”.  (See:
Zhang v. Chau
,

2003 CanLII 75292 (QC CA)
, [2003] J.Q. No. 8071, 229 D.L.R. (4
th
) 298 (C.A.) at para.
24
.)  The Ontario Court of Appeal has found that an order specifying that a
mother have supervised access until she had a “clean bill of health” to be too
vague to be enforceable.  (See:
M. (A.C.) v. M. (D.)
(2003),
2003 CanLII 18880 (ON CA)
, 67 O.R.
(3d) 181 (C.A.) at paras.
19-21
.)

[
171
]

In my view, such an order as proposed by the husband regarding the use
of the children as “go betweens” is too vague and unenforceable.  Who is going
to determine what the inflammatory issues are between the parties?  For
instance, one party may think that an issue is inflammatory and the other does
not.  Again, who will determine what is factually contentious?  What is
factually contentious to one party may not be to the other.

[
172
]

Further, how would the parties know what is to be well received or not
well received by the child?  Does the party have to say to himself or herself
every time he or she raises something with a child – will this be well received
by R. or not?  Whether or not something is well received could only be
determined after the subject is raised with the child and the damage has been
done (or not).

[
173
]

Lastly, what happens when one of the parties says that he or she needs
to discuss the subject with the other party but the child does not cease
further discussion regarding that matter?  Will the parent be in breach of the
order because the child continues to discuss this matter?   In light of the
fact that the order requested is utterly vague, there will be no order as
requested by the husband in this regard.

[
174
]

Despite the fact that I am not inclined to grant the order, I trust that
both parents will use their common sense and not use the children as messengers
to discuss important items such as the access schedule or proposed changes to
it.  Such discussions may only result in disappointed children if they are not
agreed upon by the parties.  This result should be avoided.

the wife be ordered to communicate any telephone messages left by the husband
to the children and encourage them to return phone calls?

175
]

The husband has testified that he is suspicious that telephone messages
left for the children are being picked up by the wife and not being

The fact that the wife passes on the messages was supported by a fax
exchange that occurred on October 9, 2009.  The husband wrote to the wife and

“I try to get him to call you back, but he is often unwilling

then gets side tracked.  He has
ADHD
and is constantly for getting [sic]
to do much of what I tell him.  This is just another thing (task) that he
forgets to do because his attention span is
so
short.  I
do

remind him, but it is up to him to call.  I cannot control everything and I

179
]

It is clear from this fax that the wife is doing her best to give J. the

[
180
]

I am concerned that if an order is made regarding the communication of
telephone messages as requested by the husband, the wife may become the subject

[
181
]

R. and J. are currently 15 and 12 years old.  It appears that they are

[
182
]

Such an order regarding telephone messages is not required in the

communicate via e-mail rather than fax?

[
183
]

Order of McWatt J. based on an income of $42,000.  He made this submission

[

[
237
]

The
Child Support Guidelines (Ontario)
sets out the parameters within
which the court is entitled to determine annual income.
Sections 16
and
17

state as follows:

“16.     Subject to sections 17-20, a parent’s or spouse’s
annual income is determined using the sources of income set out under the
heading “Total income” in the T1 General form issued by the Canada Revenue
Agency and is adjusted in accordance with Schedule III. …

17.(1)   If the court is of the opinion that the determination
of a parent’s or spouse’s annual income under section 16 would not be the
fairest determination of that income, the court may have regard to the parent’s
or spouse’s income over the last three years and determine an amount that is
fair and reasonable in light of any pattern of income, fluctuation in income or
receipt of a non-recurring amount during those years. …”

[
238
]

It is my view that it would be appropriate to determine the husband’s
annual income in accordance with
section 16
of the
Child Support Guidelines
.
Such a calculation is the fairest determination of the husband’s income which
in 2008 was reported as $31,883.68.  In 2007 the husband’s income was reported
as $38,133 and in 2006 it was a little over $17,000.

[
239
]

There was no suggestion made to either the husband or his accountant,
Mr. David Steingart, that there are expenses shown on his tax returns that were
not legitimate, nor was there a suggestion that the husband was committing a
tax fraud on the Canada Revenue Agency.

[
240
]

Lastly, there was no suggestion that the husband’s lifestyle was
disproportionate to his income.  Although he is currently driving a convertible
BMW with a value of approximately $60,000 and he took a two week vacation to Hawaii in January, 2009, I accept that both of these items were funded by his mother as the
husband testified.

[
241
]

The wife produced an expert at this trial by the name of Mr. Damian A.
Alksnis of MG Forensic Accounting & Investigations Inc.  He was qualified
to give evidence about the preparation of the husband’s tax returns and the
level of income that was reported in them.  Mr. Alksnis suggested that based
upon the information that was made available to him from the wife and the
disclosure provided, the husband would require $145,000 to carry the debt
incurred by him.

[
242
]

However, in cross examination, Mr. Alksnis conceded that he was not
aware that between 2005 and 2007, the husband obtained an equity take out on
his Beaty property which would explain some of the cash deficit calculated by
Mr. Alksnis.  He testified that this would alleviate concerns that he had about
such a debt load being carried by the husband.  Further, Mr. Alksnis conceded
that he attributed an expense of $4,800 for school tuition from 2004 to 2007
that was not incurred by the husband.  He also included in his calculation,
household expenses in the amount of $300; home repairs in the amount of $600
and $2,700 for electricity for 2004-2006 which were not incurred by the
husband.  Mr. Alsknis also testified that he was not aware that the husband had
a sub-tenant in his home commencing in 2007 that would have reduced his living
expense.

[
243
]

Based upon the evidence given in cross-examination, approximately
$55,000 would have to be removed from Mr. Alksnis’ calculation regarding the
husband’s expenses.  That, together with the $180,000 equity take out would
indicate that the calculations by Mr. Alksnis regarding the income that the
husband must have to sustain his debts was inaccurate.  Accordingly, I cannot
conclude that the husband requires $145,000 to service his debts.

[
244
]

It was suggested to Mr. Aksnis that the husband did not provide proper
disclosure.  However, Mr. Alksnis testified that he relied upon information
provided by the wife and the disclosure provided pursuant to the orders of the
court.  There was no suggestion made, whatsoever, that the husband was in
breach of any court order regarding disclosure and I accept that he was not.

[
245
]

There was evidence before the Court to suggest that the husband had
inflated his income on a credit card application to RBC in the summer of 2008.
In that application, he stated that he earned an annual income of $150,000.
This, according to the husband, was a lie in order to obtain greater credit.  I
accept that evidence and I accept that the husband has not earned income even
close to $150,000 in the last three years as set out above.  Although I do not
condone such behaviour, Mr. Alksnis testified that this would not be the first
time that he had seen somebody exaggerate how much money they earn on a credit
card application to secure greater credit.  Accordingly, I do not accept the
income of the husband as set out in the credit card application as a basis to
conclude he was earning $150,000 in 2008.

[
246
]

Based upon the history of the marriage and the husband’s ability to earn
income, there is no reason to impute income to him.  The wife testified,
herself, that during the marriage, the husband’s employment was almost
“non-existent”.  She believes that the husband was only employed for about
three years and his investments were sporadic.  He would make investments and
he would usually lose money on those investments as he made poor decisions.  I
accept the evidence of the husband that not much as changed since the parties
separated in June, 2003.

[
247
]

There was one year during the marriage that the husband earned a healthy
living when he was employed as an appliance salesman at Home and Rural.  In
that year, he earned approximately $75,000 but he was laid off.  However, this
year in the life of the marriage of the parties was exceptional.  Otherwise,
the parties were living in a rented home, relying on the generosity of Mrs.
D.N. (the husband’s mother) and shopping at Goodwill.  They did not accumulate
any savings.  There were no contributions made to RRSP’s or RESP’s during their
marriage.  On the date of separation, the husband had gross debts of $487,000.

[
248
]

There was no evidence provided to the court that the husband should have
income imputed to him in the amount of $60,000 to $70,000 per year.
Accordingly, child support will be paid by the husband in accordance with the
income set out by McWatt J. in 2004 which is $42,000 per year.

Should

1.

Despite the acrimony between the parties in this litigation, it is my

parties) that access is set up so that it is fair to all and that the
requirement for communication between the parties is minimal.

After hearing the submissions of both parties, they were almost
identical in their proposal for access to the children.  The wife was mainly

the access schedule.

5.

division of hours between the parties, it is my view that it is more important
to set the pick up and drop off times.  I am hoping that this will alleviate
any tension between the parties when communicating about access.  It is my view
that communication must be minimized between the parties to avoid any hostility
that the children may witness.

Should the wife be entitled
to move her residence and if so, should there be a geographical limitation
on such a move?  What should the driving arrangements be for the access
visits should the wife move homes?

1.

The husband is agreeable that the wife be able to move her residence
with the children.  However, he is of the view that she should be restrained
from moving any further than 25 kilometres from her current residence.  He also
submits that she should be responsible for retrieving the children from his
home during any mid week access visits and on Sundays when weekend access ends.

2.

The wife submits that the move that she is contemplating is either 22
kilometres (to Waterdown) or 30 kilometres (to Burlington).   The purpose of
moving is so that she is closer to J.’s school and friends.  She has also
submitted that she is required to move for financial reasons.  The move that
the wife is contemplating will provide the family with more affordable housing
and allow her to reduce some of the family debts.  I accept her evidence in
this regard.

3.

I am of the view that the wife should be entitled to move to either of
the locations proposed and within 35 kilometres of her current residence.  The
distance between the homes is not great and the reasons for moving appear to be
legitimate.  The driving arrangements should remain as described above should
she do so.

4.

The husband expressed concern about the wife being responsible for
getting the children to his home on time for his access visits.  Although there
appeared to be some issues at the commencement of the separation (June, 2003) I
did not hear much evidence about late delivery in the recent past.

5.

To satisfy the husband’s concerns about the wife’s late delivery of the
children, I have ordered that he will be the one responsible for picking up the
children for each access visit to ensure that he has the time with the children
that has been allotted to him.  If he had not expressed such concern about the
wife’s inability to deliver the children on time, I would have ordered that the
wife deliver the children to his home for mid week access but that is not the
case.

6.

In my view, it only makes sense that the husband take the children to
school, camp or the wife’s home following his mid week access visits.  He is
already driving J. to school in Burlington after his mid week access visits.
Further, he is not currently working in a job outside of the home and his hours
appear flexible so that he is in a position to drive them.  Such a drive would
also allow him more time with each child in an environment where he can
communicate with them without much distraction.

7.

I do agree that the wife should be responsible for some of the driving.
She will be picking up the children after each weekend visit and as indicated
during the holiday times.  This order is imposed regardless of where she is
living.

8.

In light of the above, an order will go allowing the wife to move within
35 kilometres of her current home.  The driving for access will be as set out
under the question regarding access above.
